title: The Grid That Keeps People Alive
subtitle: How likely is it? How bad would it be? Two questions that decide what hospitals, airlines and engineers worry about first.

card.essence: You cannot prevent everything. So safety experts score every danger twice — how likely, and how serious — and act on the red corner first. It is the most-used grid in the working world.

intention: you'll learn how safety teams decide what to worry about, score six real risks yourself, and practise the language of probability: likely to, may well, bound to, unlikely.
warmup: What is the most dangerous thing you do in a normal week? Do you think about it?
Are people good at judging danger? Think about flying, driving and swimming.
In your job or home, who decides what is safe?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: The engineers listed every hazard on the site: deep water, moving vehicles, electricity.
items.meaning: hazard — something that could cause harm or damage.

items.sent: A small fire is annoying; a fire in the fuel store would be catastrophic.
Wearing a helmet does not remove the danger, but it does reduce the harm.
items.meaning: reduce — to make something smaller or less.

items.sent: Nurses must report every near miss — an accident that almost happened.
items.meaning: near miss — a situation where something bad nearly happened but didn't.

vocab.heading: B · Which word matches the meaning?
vocab.intro: The three words are: likelihood · consequence · precaution. Read each meaning, say the word, then reveal.

items.sent: (noun) Something you do in advance to stop a problem happening.
(noun) The chance that something will happen.
(noun) The result of an action, especially a bad one.

vocab.heading: C · Which word completes all three phrases?
vocab.intro: One missing word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.sent: take a ___  ·  a high-___ patient  ·  at ___ of losing everything
items.meaning: risk — the chance that something bad happens; a dangerous situation.

items.sent: ___ an accident  ·  ___ the spread of a disease  ·  better to ___ than to cure
a safety ___  ·  run through the ___ before take-off  ·  tick the ___

vocab_use: What precautions do you take without thinking — at home, at work, on the road?
Tell us about a near miss you remember.
Which everyday risk do you think people worry about too much?

story.heading: Part 1 — You cannot prevent everything
paras: Imagine you run a small hospital. This morning your list of worries includes a broken lift, a nurse shortage at night, a cupboard of medicines with similar-looking boxes, a leaking roof, and a computer system that is ten years old.
You cannot fix all of them today. So which one do you start with? The loudest complaint? The cheapest repair? The one in yesterday's newspaper?

Through the twentieth century, industries that could kill people — mining, chemicals, nuclear power, aviation — learned an uncomfortable lesson. You can never remove every hazard. What you can do is be honest about which hazards deserve your money and your attention first. And for that, you need to ask about each one not one question but two.
checks: Why can't the hospital fix everything?
Which industries learned this lesson first?
How many questions does each hazard need?
answers: There isn't enough time or money — you have to choose.
Dangerous ones: mining, chemicals, nuclear power, aviation.
story.discuss: In your workplace or home, how do people usually decide what to fix first?

story.heading: Part 2 — Two questions, one grid
paras: The two questions are these. How likely is it to happen? And how bad would it be if it did?

Answer both — usually on a scale from low to high — and every hazard lands in a box on a grid. The bottom-left corner holds things that probably won't happen and wouldn't matter much. The top-right corner holds things that are likely and would be catastrophic. That corner gets your money, today.

The grid also solves an old argument. People disagree loudly about danger, because they are usually arguing about different questions. One person is thinking about likelihood (“that has never happened here”), the other about consequence (“if it did, someone would die”). The grid makes them answer both questions separately, and suddenly the argument becomes a conversation.
Its power is that it works for a nuclear plant, a school trip or a wedding.
checks: Which corner of the grid gets attention first?
Why do people argue about danger, according to the story?
answers: How likely is it? How bad would it be?
Because they are answering different questions — one thinks about likelihood, the other about consequence.
story.discuss: Think of an argument you've heard about safety. Were the two sides answering different questions?

story.heading: Part 3 — The rare and the terrible
paras: The grid has a famous weak spot: the box where something is very unlikely but would be catastrophic. A huge flood. A new disease. A bank collapsing. Because the likelihood is low, these risks sit quietly in a corner of the page for years — until the year they don't.

There is a second problem. The numbers look scientific, but somebody chose them. Give the same hazard to two teams and they will often score it differently, especially when the person scoring it is also the person who would have to pay for the repair.

So good teams use the grid as the start of a conversation, not the end of one. They add a rule: anything that could kill someone gets attention whatever its score. And they record the near misses, because a near miss is the cheapest warning you will ever get.
checks: Which box is the famous weak spot?
Why can two teams score the same hazard differently?
What extra rule do good teams add?
answers: Because the scores are human judgements — and the scorer may be the person who would pay for the repair.
Anything that could kill someone gets attention whatever its score (and they record near misses).
story.discuss: How should a company plan for something that is very unlikely but terrible?

tool_tab.lead: Score each hazard twice. Along the bottom: how likely is it? Up the side: how serious would it be? The colour of the box tells you how fast to act.
how: List the hazards plainly — what could go wrong, and to whom.
Score each one for likelihood, using evidence: has it happened here before? How often?
Score each one for consequence: the realistic worst case, not the imaginable worst case.
Start at the red corner. For each one, either reduce the likelihood, reduce the harm, or both — then score it again.

sort.intro: A language school is planning a day trip to the mountains. Which box does each risk belong in? Choose, then check.

items.text: Rain during the walk. It rains most weeks, and everyone would get wet and uncomfortable.
items.why: very likely, but only a minor consequence.

items.text: A student with a serious nut allergy is given the wrong packed lunch. The kitchen prepares them by hand, and this nearly happened last term.
items.why: likely (it nearly happened already) and possibly fatal.

items.text: The bus breaks down on the mountain road. The company's buses are old and it happened last year; the group would be stuck for hours in the cold.
items.why: likely, and the consequences are serious.

items.text: A student twists an ankle on the path. It happens on about one trip in three, and means a slow walk back.
items.why: fairly likely; painful but not severe.
catastrophic, but so rare that no plan is possible.
it may well happen, but it is easily fixed.

breaks: The scores are opinions in disguise. Two honest teams often score the same hazard differently.
The rare-but-terrible box. Low likelihood pushes real dangers off the page for years.
It can become paperwork. A finished grid is not a safer school — the actions are.
discuss: Which risk on the trip would you spend money on first?
Should the person who pays for repairs be the person who scores the risks?

grammar.name: likely, may well, bound to
grammar.lead: This grid runs on probability. English has a rich set of ways to say how likely something is — far beyond maybe.
notes:
be likely / unlikely + to + verb — the everyday way to score a chance.
“Prices are likely to rise next year.”  “He is unlikely to pass without help.”
Also: “It is likely that prices will rise.”

may well / might well — a real possibility, stronger than may.
“The meeting may well finish early.”

be bound to / be sure to — you are almost certain.
“With this traffic, we are bound to be late.”

There's a good / slight chance (that)…
“There's a slight chance of snow.”
Watch out: likely is an adjective, not a verb: ~~It likely to rain~~ → “It is likely to rain.” And after bound to we use the bare verb: “bound to be late”.

exercises.heading: Complete the sentences
exercises.intro: Write one word in each gap.
items: 1. The road is closed, so the bus is ___ to be late — I'd say ninety-nine per cent.
2. Older machines are more ___ to break down than new ones.
3. There's a slight ___ of frost tonight, so cover the plants.
4. She may ___ refuse the offer — she's turned down two already.
5. It is ___ that the flight will be cancelled; the storm is enormous.

exercises.heading: Score the risk in words
exercises.intro: Rewrite each sentence with the words in brackets, keeping the meaning.
items: 1. It will probably rain during the walk. (likely) → Rain ___
2. There is almost no chance of a meteorite. (unlikely) → A meteorite ___
3. Perhaps the bus will break down — it has before. (may well) → The bus ___
4. With no map, we will certainly get lost. (bound) → Without a map, we ___
answers: 1. Rain is likely (to fall) during the walk.
2. A meteorite is extremely unlikely (to hit us).
4. Without a map, we are bound to get lost.

grammar.closing: Now score three risks in your own life or work: one likely, one unlikely, one you are bound to face.

speak.intro: Use the grid on something real. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk. Use the probability language from the grammar tab.
speak.useful: “That's likely, but not serious.” · “It's unlikely — however, if it happened, …” · “We're bound to …” · “I'd put that in the red corner because …”

tasks.label: Task 1 — Your place
paras: Think of your home, workplace or journey to work. Name three risks and score each one on both questions.

tasks.label: Task 2 — The rare and terrible
paras: Name something very unlikely that would be very serious for you. What, if anything, do you do about it?

tasks.label: Task 3 — Convince someone
paras: Someone dismisses a danger you take seriously. Explain your scoring and try to change their mind.

final: Governments use this grid for floods and pandemics. Why do the rare-but-terrible risks still surprise us?
Is it acceptable to put a price on reducing a risk to human life? Argue both ways, then commit.
Do people judge risk better from numbers or from stories? Which changes your own behaviour?
From memory: describe three risks on the school trip using likely to, may well and bound to.
